title: Multilingual sites without a mess
excerpt: Translate the offer, not only the menus. Give each language its own URL. A toggle that hides pages you never translated will strand the reader.
alt: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table. The meeting around a layout fits a piece about keeping each language's pages whole.
caption: Each language needs a full page, not a costume. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How should a small site structure two languages?
faqs.answer: Give each language its own URLs, and translate the offer, not only the navigation. A path or subdomain that stays stable is enough. The homepage, the primary action, and the key proof should exist in both languages before you add a language switcher. A switcher that lands on an untranslated page is a trap.

faqs.question: Is a translation widget enough?
faqs.answer: No. An automatic overlay that rewrites the chrome and leaves the pitch in the original language, or that hides pages it cannot translate, makes the site look finished and read broken. Write the pages you mean to support. Google's title-link guidance also says the title should match the language of the page, so a translated title on an untranslated body is a mismatch in both directions.

faqs.question: What should stay shared across languages?
faqs.answer: The product, the price logic, and the facts. Names of people and products usually stay as they are, while the sentence that explains them changes. Design tokens, layout, and the booking path should be shared so you do not maintain two brands. Content and URLs should not be shared if the reader is promised a language you did not actually write.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
Translate the offer, not only the chrome. Give each language a real URL. A toggle that hides untranslated pages is a trap. That is a workable multilingual website structure for a small company. The menu in another language, sitting on top of the same English pitch, is a costume. The reader notices in the first sentence.

Pick the languages you will actually maintain. One extra language, done properly, is a second site in the ways that matter and the same site in the ways that should stay shared. Two half-finished languages are a mess you will be ashamed to send.

## Translate the offer

The offer is the headline, the description of the work, the primary action, and the proof a buyer needs. Those have to exist in the target language as real sentences, written by someone who can hear when they are wrong. Translating "Home," "About," and "Contact," and leaving the hero in the original language, is the common failure. The chrome looks local. The company does not.

Write fresh where the language needs it. A literal word-for-word pass keeps idioms that do not travel and keeps a word order that sounds machine-made. You want the same claim, in a sentence a native reader would say. The founder, or a writer they trust in that language, has to approve the offer. A vendor pass with no reviewer will be confident and slightly off, which is worse than obviously unfinished.

Names, prices, and legal facts do not get "creative" translation. The company name stays. The price, if you show it, stays true. The privacy policy has to be a real policy in that language if you are asking people there to submit a form. Linking a translated form to an untranslated policy, or the reverse, splits the promise. Do the pair together or do not launch the form.

Google's people-first guidance asks whether a reader leaves having learned enough, or whether they have to search again for a better explanation. A half-translated page sends them back to search, often in the language you just failed. That is the test. If a reader in the second language still cannot say what you do, you do not have a second-language site. You have a switcher.

## A real URL for each language

Give every translated page its own address. A path prefix is a clear pattern: the same slugs, under a language segment, with the original language either at the root or under its own prefix. Pick one pattern and keep it. What matters is that a person can copy a link and land on the language they were reading, and that a search result can point at that language directly.

Do not store the language only in a cookie or a session toggle. A link that opens in whatever language the last visitor used is a broken link. The URL is the contract. The toggle can set a preference. It should also navigate to the matching URL. If the matching URL does not exist, the toggle should not pretend it does.

Titles have to match the page. Google's documentation on title links says to use the same language and writing system as the primary content. A page whose body is in French and whose title is an English keyword string is a mismatch, and Google may replace the title. Write the title in the language of the page. Do the same for the main heading. A reader who arrived from search should see the language they were promised before they scroll.

Tell search engines about the alternates in a consistent way, with a single preferred URL for each language, and avoid publishing the same translation at two addresses. Duplicate language URLs split the signals and confuse the toggle. One page, one address, linked to its partners. That is enough structure for a small site. You do not need a complex detection maze on the first request. If you guess a language from the browser, redirect only when you are confident, and always leave a way back. A wrong automatic redirect is a trap with confidence.

## The toggle that hides a hole

A switcher implies a destination. If the destination is the homepage in the other language, say so, or do not offer the switch on pages you have not translated. Dropping a reader on a generic home, or hiding the page and showing a message, breaks the task they were in the middle of. They were on a project, or a price, or a post. Send them to the translated version of that page, or leave them where they are and do not wave a language you cannot deliver.

Do not hide untranslated pages from the navigation in one language and leave them in the XML of the other, or the reverse, without a plan. The public nav, the footer, and the sitemap should agree about what exists. A page that exists only as a URL you hope nobody finds will be found. Either translate it, or keep it out of that language's index and out of that language's links.

Machine translation in the browser, as a widget that rewrites the DOM, fails this test quietly. It does not give you a URL. It does not give you a reviewable sentence. It drifts when you change a heading. It often misses the text baked into images. Use it as a private draft if you must, then replace it with a page a human approved. Do not ship the widget as the product.

Images with words in them need a version per language or, better, the words need to come out of the image and into HTML. A hero that is a picture of an English headline will keep speaking English after the most careful translation of the paragraph under it. That bug looks like carelessness because it is.

## What stays shared

The layout, the type, the color, and the components stay shared. You are not designing a second brand. You are filling the same system with a second text. Watch for strings that were drawn as part of a component and never extracted. Buttons, errors, empty states, form labels, the cookie banner, the confirmation page. Those are the offer too. A translated hero with an English "Submit" is a half page.

Length changes. German and French runs will break a heading that was tuned for a short English line. Design the heading to wrap. Do not shrink the type until it fits one language and becomes unreadable in the other. The measure of a long article still has to be comfortable after the expansion. Test with the real copy, not with "lorem" of the same length as the English.

Right-to-left languages, if you take one on, are a layout project, not a string project. Navigation, alignment, and icons that imply direction have to flip with care. Do not start that in the same week as your first Latin-script translation unless you have the design time. Scope is how these projects stay clean.

The booking path and the contact path should be shared logic with translated text. A form that posts to the same place, with a field that records the language, lets you reply in the right language. A form that only exists in one language, linked from another, tells the reader the second language was a brochure. If you cannot support the conversation in that language, do not imply the form is local. Say which language you will reply in.

## Navigation and the way back

The language control should be a real control, with a name, in the header, showing the current language as text. Flags are a poor substitute. Languages are not countries. A flag will be wrong for someone who speaks the language outside that flag's borders, and it is a tiny target. Use the name of the language, in that language, so a person who cannot read the current page can still find the switch.

When they switch, keep them on the equivalent page. When there is no equivalent, stay put and do not offer the switch, or offer it with a clear landing you have written: a short page that says the detailed piece is only in the other language and here is the offer in this one. That short page is a real URL. It is honest. A silent failure is not.

Internal links have to stay in the language. An article that links back to the English service page from a translated paragraph yanks the reader out of the language you just promised. Build the links from the translated slugs. This is the part teams forget, and it is the part that makes the site feel random. Audit a language by clicking, not by scanning the dictionary file.

Search on the site, if you have it, should search the language the person is in, or clearly mark results from the other. Mixed results without labels look like duplicate pages and broken translation. For a small marketing site you may not need search at all. Do not add it only for the second language.

## A scope for the first second language

List the pages that must exist before you announce the language. Usually: home, the offer, the proof, the contact or booking page, and the privacy page if you collect anything. Journal posts can remain in the original language until you choose to translate one, as long as you do not link them as if they were translated. Say, in the second language, that the journal is in the first, if you link it at all.

Assign an owner who can read the language. Publishing without an owner is how the second site rots. The owner reviews changes to the offer in both languages in the same week. A price change, a new project, a renamed service: both URLs update, or the language you did not update gets a note. Stale translation is a false offer.

Do not launch on a hard date because a campaign is translated and the site is not. Send the campaign to the pages that exist. A localized ad into an English-only site is a broken promise you paid to run. The structure is what makes the campaign tell the truth.

Next.js can express a language in the route and share the components. The repository can hold both texts next to each other so a change is reviewable. None of that writes the sentences. Budget the writing. The engineering is the smaller risk.

[Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) shows the kind of single-language clarity a second language has to earn again, page by page. The structure is a copy of the offer, not a skin on the nav.

After a redesign, including one that adds languages and new URLs, you will want to know what searchers still find. [Search console after a redesign](/blog/search-console-after-a-redesign) is the next piece, on watching the queries, the pages that fell, and the redirects before you change the site again.
